Dermatology · published research

Pemphigus vegetans

One case report describes rapid plaque improvement with red light added to corticosteroids, but it cannot isolate the light effect. Small reports in pemphigus vulgaris concern a different subtype and provide only indirect supporting evidence.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

One case report describes rapid plaque improvement with red light added to corticosteroids, but it cannot isolate the light effect. Small reports in pemphigus vulgaris concern a different subtype and provide only indirect supporting evidence.

Summary of the Evidence

Four publications are relevant only when a narrow mapping is used: one case report directly describes pemphigus vegetans, while three records concern pemphigus vulgaris, a related but distinct autoimmune blistering disease. The mapped records include a 10-person pilot, a two-case report, and a review. They do not constitute direct clinical evidence for pemphigus vegetans, and the reports do not indicate a shared cohort.

Human and clinical evidence

The exact-condition publication is a single case report. It describes rapid improvement in pemphigus vegetans plaques after 640-nm high-fluence red visible light was added to low-dose methylprednisolone. Because light and corticosteroid were started together, the report cannot determine how much improvement came from either treatment or from the course of the disease (Wang et al. 2020).

The mapped pemphigus vulgaris pilot enrolled ten people and compared laser-treated lesions with conventionally managed lesions. It reported improved lesion or wound scores in the treated areas, but the findings concern pemphigus vulgaris, not pemphigus vegetans, and do not establish an effect on systemic disease activity (Yousefi et al. 2017). A two-case report described use of low-level laser therapy alongside systemic treatment for oral and cutaneous lesions; it cannot separate the light effect from concurrent care (Minicucci et al. 2012). A review summarizes this limited related literature but does not add a new patient cohort.

Animal evidence

No animal study directly relevant to pemphigus vegetans or the mapped pemphigus vulgaris records was identified.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No disease-specific cell or ex-vivo study was identified in this category.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The direct case used 640-nm red visible light at high fluence with corticosteroid treatment. The mapped reports used low-level red laser protocols, including 660-nm light in the pilot, but their parameters and lesion-level co-treatments differ. No comparison establishes an optimal wavelength or dose, and data from pemphigus vulgaris should not be treated as though they tested pemphigus vegetans.

Interpretation

The direct case documents improvement during combined treatment, and related pemphigus vulgaris reports describe lesion-level benefits with adjunctive light. These observations give a reason to study local symptom and wound outcomes, but they do not establish PBM efficacy for pemphigus vegetans or control of the underlying autoimmune disease.

Evidence strength in source summaryVery low for direct evidence in pemphigus vegetans Very low for adjunctive lesion improvement in related pemphigus vulgaris
Publications and records4 articles (3 mapped from pemphigus vulgaris)

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

The only report directly involving pemphigus vegetans is one case in which red light was added to corticosteroid treatment, so the separate contribution of light cannot be measured. Three mapped records concern pemphigus vulgaris, a related but distinct subtype, and also combine light with other care. Controlled studies in pemphigus vegetans with separate lesion and symptom outcomes would be needed for a stronger conclusion.
